part1_forecasts.statement: The US will generate at least $50 billion in cumulative tariff revenue from advanced AI chips not designated for domestic supply chains by the end of 2027.

resolution_criteria.metric: cumulative tariff revenue from advanced AI chips
resolution_criteria.counting_convention: USD, collected revenue from imports subject to the 25% tariff, measured annually

part1_forecasts.statement: China's Ministry of Commerce will announce at least one new set of restrictions on specific rare earth element applications by mid-2028.

resolution_criteria.metric: number of new rare earth export control announcements targeting specific applications
resolution_criteria.counting_convention: announcements, in-force regulations impacting specific end-uses

resolution_criteria.source: Global Trade Alert (New Industrial Policy Observatory - NIPO)
resolution_criteria.metric: annual count of state-led industrial policy interventions
resolution_criteria.counting_convention: count, new interventions registered annually, encompassing all types

resolution_criteria.source: European Commission Directorate-General for Internal Market, Industry, Entrepreneurship and SMEs
resolution_criteria.metric: average year-over-year cost increase for critical micro-transistor components for EU automotive manufacturers

resolution_criteria.counting_convention: percentage increase, measured annually from baseline cost

part1_forecasts.statement: The US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) will issue at least one new regulation further restricting the export of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment to China by early 2029.

resolution_criteria.metric: average annual global nominal GDP growth

resolution_criteria.counting_convention: percentage points, measured as a compounded annual growth rate over the specified period

resolution_criteria.source: U.S. Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
resolution_criteria.metric: duration of 'case-by-case review' policy for advanced AI chips to China

part1_forecasts.statement: China will not domestically produce a competitive alternative to the NVIDIA H200 chip by August 2031, indicated by fewer than 50 new foundational patent filings for comparable architecture.

resolution_criteria.metric: number of new foundational patent filings for AI accelerator chips comparable to NVIDIA H200
resolution_criteria.counting_convention: patent filings, per annum, for technologies exhibiting equivalent compute and memory bandwidth

part2_framework.text:
The current global landscape is defined by a fierce, modern mercantilist struggle for dominance in Artificial Intelligence (AI), driven by nations leveraging industrial policy and trade controls to secure national power and economic advantage. At its core, this struggle is a zero-sum game where the United States, currently holding an overwhelming advantage in global AI compute (E05), is actively employing a dual strategy to maintain and extend its lead, while China and other actors seek to counter or circumvent these efforts.

The U.S. has fundamentally altered its trade strategy, moving away from traditional Most Favored Nation (MFN) frameworks towards a more assertive, mercantilist approach characterized by systematic tariffs and deficit reduction targets (E12). This shift is not merely economic; it's a direct manifestation of statecraft aimed at consolidating national power through technological superiority, particularly in AI. The U.S. 2025 AI Action Plan exemplifies this, formalizing a two-pronged sovereign AI framework. This framework prioritizes expanding domestic capabilities—semiconductor manufacturing, data center capacity, and energy infrastructure—while simultaneously exporting a comprehensive American AI technology package internationally (E10).

This aggressive pursuit of AI sovereignty has led to direct interventions in the global chip market. The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has implemented regulations that, while sometimes shifting from outright denial to case-by-case review for certain advanced chips destined for China (E01), are ultimately designed to control the flow of critical AI hardware. Furthermore, a U.S. Presidential Proclamation in January 2026 imposed a significant 25% tariff on imported advanced AI chips not intended for the domestic U.S. supply chain (E02), a clear mercantilist tool to incentivize domestic production and consumption while penalizing foreign reliance.

These controls are not abstract; they have tangible impacts on supply chains and market dynamics. For instance, Chinese customers are now restricted from acquiring more than 50% of the total NVIDIA H200 chip volume sold to American customers, a measure requiring independent third-party testing for shipments (E03). This is a deliberate attempt to limit China's access to cutting-edge AI accelerators, thereby hobbling its own AI development and maintaining the U.S. compute advantage (E05).

China, in response to U.S. actions and to bolster its own industrial base, has also resorted to export controls, particularly concerning critical resources. The addition of five rare earth elements to its export control list and the assertion of global regulatory authority over products containing Chinese-sourced materials (E04) demonstrate a retaliatory strategy. This also extends to semiconductors, as seen in October 2025 when Beijing restricted exports from a Dutch-owned chipmaker with a Chinese subsidiary supplying critical components to European automakers (E11). This highlights the complex, interconnected nature of modern mercantilism, where actions in one sector or region can trigger ripple effects across global supply chains and create difficult choices for other nations.

The broader trend of state-led industrial policy interventions, accelerated by frameworks like the U.S. CHIPS Act and IRA, has become a dominant feature of the global economy. These interventions, driven by national security and supply security objectives, have intensified through 2025 (E06). This state-centric approach to economic management is creating a bifurcated global market, with regions like Europe often caught between competing U.S. and Chinese demands and restrictions.

The consequences of this intensified mercantilism are significant. Mid-2026 economic updates point to a combination of modern mercantilism and AI infrastructure investment driving higher-than-target nominal GDP growth. However, this growth is accompanied by acute resource and commodity constraints (E08), underscoring the cost and potential unsustainability of this high-stakes competition. Nations are prioritizing national advantage, even at the expense of global efficiency or collaborative development.

This framework is not static. The U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee's advancement of export control legislation, including the Chip Security Act in April 2026, aimed at curbing diversions of AI semiconductors to adversaries (E07), indicates a continued governmental focus on tightening controls. The establishment of national AI offices, such as Malaysia's NAIO in late 2024 overseeing a national AI technology action plan spanning 2026–2030 (E09), shows other nations actively developing their own strategies within this new paradigm.

In conclusion, the current era is characterized by a deliberate, state-driven reshaping of trade and industrial policy, inextricably linked to the advancement of AI. The U.S. is proactively defending and expanding its AI supremacy through a mercantilist framework of tariffs and export controls, while China retaliates with its own strategic resource and industrial controls. This creates a volatile global market where national power is increasingly equated with AI dominance, pushing nations to prioritize self-sufficiency and technological advantage above all else, with significant economic and geopolitical repercussions for those not at the forefront of this AI race.
cause_effect_dynamics: D1: U.S. imposition of tariffs on imported advanced AI chips (E02) -> reduced attractiveness of foreign AI chips for domestic supply chain (Implicit from E02) because the tariffs make them more expensive for non-domestic use.
D2: U.S. conditional export framework on NVIDIA H200 chips to China (E03) -> limitations on Chinese access to advanced AI hardware (E03) because of volume caps and testing requirements.

D3: U.S. dual-pronged sovereign AI framework prioritizing domestic expansion and AI tech export (E10) -> U.S. control of global AI compute advantage (E05) because it bolsters domestic capabilities while influencing international markets.

D4: China's addition of rare earth elements to export control list (E04) and restriction of Dutch chipmaker exports (E11) -> global trade retaliation and supply chain disruptions (Implicit from E04, E11) as other nations are impacted by these controls.

D5: U.S. shift from MFN frameworks to mercantilist tariffs and deficit targets (E12) -> systematic leveraging of trade as a core lever of statecraft (E12) because these tools are directly employed to achieve national power objectives.

D6: Expansion of state-led industrial policy interventions (E06) -> accelerated pursuit of national security and supply security objectives (E06) as governments increasingly use these policies to fortify their economies and defenses.

D7: Modern mercantilism combined with AI infrastructure investment (E08) -> sustained higher-than-target nominal GDP growth alongside acute resource and commodity constraints (E08) because economic expansion is driven by state intervention but faces inherent resource limitations.

F01.reasoning: The current US share of global AI compute at 75% (E05) significantly exceeds the forecast threshold of 65% for August 2027. The US's stated policy of expanding domestic capacity and exporting a full-stack AI technology package (E10) further supports this dominance. China's current share is 15% (E05), well below the 20% forecast limit. While China is actively developing its AI capabilities, the US's lead in hardware, investment, and export control policies (E01, E06) makes maintaining its significant lead highly probable. A significant shift would require a substantial acceleration in China's domestic production and a loosening of US export controls.

F02.reasoning: The Presidential Proclamation imposing a 25% tariff on advanced AI chips not intended for the domestic US supply chain (E02) provides a direct mechanism for generating tariff revenue. Given the significant global market for AI chips, even with restrictions, a cumulative $50 billion in revenue by the end of 2027 is plausible, especially considering the ongoing US efforts to curb Chinese access (E07). The probability is moderate because the actual revenue will depend on the volume of targeted chips that flow through these trade channels and the effectiveness of enforcement. A decline in global AI chip demand or a significant circumvention of these tariffs by China would lower this probability.

F03.reasoning: China's Ministry of Commerce has already demonstrated a willingness to implement export controls on rare earth elements (E04) and has asserted regulatory authority over foreign-made products containing Chinese-sourced materials. This precedent, combined with the ongoing global competition for strategic resources, makes it highly likely that China will announce further restrictions on specific rare earth element applications by mid-2028. The dynamic (D4) suggests a responsive action to geopolitical pressures. A lower probability would be influenced by a significant de-escalation in US-China trade tensions or a breakthrough in alternative material sourcing by global manufacturers.

F04.reasoning: The accelerating trend of state-led industrial policy interventions, originating around 2020 and expanding through initiatives like the US CHIPS Act and IRA (E06), is projected to continue. The focus on national security and supply security objectives (E06) further fuels this trend. The dynamic (D6) indicates a continued expansion of these interventions globally. The forecast of a 15% increase from 2025 levels by the end of 2027 aligns with this trajectory. A lower probability would arise if geopolitical tensions de-escalated significantly, leading to a reduction in national security-driven industrial policies.

F05.reasoning: The evidence indicates that Beijing has restricted exports from a Dutch-owned chipmaker whose subsidiary supplies micro-transistors to European automotive manufacturers (E11). This exemplifies how Chinese industrial policy and trade retaliation can intersect with global supply chains. Coupled with concurrent US trade policies (implied by E08 and E12), which are described as 'modern mercantilism' and deficit reduction targets, it is plausible that European automotive manufacturers will face cost increases for critical components. The dynamic (D4) suggests a response to trade policies. A lower probability would be if trade policies were significantly relaxed or if European manufacturers found readily available, cost-competitive alternative suppliers outside of these geopolitical pressures.

F06.reasoning: The US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has already implemented measures restricting exports of advanced AI chips to China (E01), shifting from a 'presumption of denial' to 'case-by-case review' which still implies significant control. Further export control legislation is also advancing (E07). The US's stated sovereign AI framework (E10) and efforts to curb technology diversion (E07) suggest a continued focus on restricting China's access to advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The dynamic (D2) suggests a sustained, restrictive policy. A lower probability would occur if the US significantly softened its stance on technology exports to China due to economic pressures or diplomatic breakthroughs.

F07.reasoning: The confluence of 'modern mercantilism' and 'AI infrastructure investment' is highlighted as driving higher-than-target nominal GDP growth (E08), while 'resource and commodity constraints' are noted as limitations. The forecast of 4.5% annual growth between mid-2026 and mid-2029 reflects this dynamic. However, the relatively low probability of 0.4 suggests that the balancing act between these growth drivers and constraints is delicate. Significant global economic shocks, unforeseen resource scarcities, or a sharp downturn in AI investment could push growth below this average, thereby lowering the probability. Conversely, a more integrated and less constrained global supply chain could boost this probability.

F08.reasoning: Malaysia's establishment of a National Artificial Intelligence Office (NAIO) (E09) serves as a model for other emerging economies seeking to structure their AI strategies. The dynamic (D5) implies a growing trend in national AI governance. Given the global focus on AI development and the desire of emerging economies to participate in and benefit from this technological wave, it is plausible that at least three new national AI offices, mirroring Malaysia's structure, will be established by the end of 2029. A lower probability would be influenced by a global economic downturn impacting these nations' ability to fund such initiatives or a shift in focus away from AI at the national policy level.

F09.reasoning: The US implemented a 'case-by-case review' policy for advanced AI chips to China on January 13, 2026 (E01), which represents a significant, albeit not absolute, restriction. The evidence points to a sustained US focus on controlling advanced AI chip exports to adversaries (E07), aligning with the dynamic (D2) of ongoing regulatory restrictions. Given the geopolitical landscape and the strategic importance of AI, it is highly probable that this policy will remain in effect for at least three full years. A significant change would likely be driven by a fundamental shift in US-China relations or a major technological breakthrough that alters the strategic calculus.

F10.reasoning: The forecast suggests China will not produce a competitive alternative to the NVIDIA H200 chip by August 2031, indicated by fewer than 50 new foundational patent filings for comparable architecture. This is strongly supported by the existing US export controls (E01, E03) that limit China's access to cutting-edge chips and manufacturing equipment (E06). The dynamic (D2) emphasizes the ongoing restrictive US policies. China's current share of global AI compute (15% in E05) and the restrictions on H200 chip volume (E03) suggest a significant lag. A higher probability would require a dramatic acceleration in China's domestic chip innovation and manufacturing capabilities, overcoming current technological and policy hurdles.
